nodes.title: Name Needed
nodes.purpose: An application needs network endpoints for a human-readable host name.

details.summary: A browser, CLI, or service starts with a host name and asks for records that can lead to an address.
what: The caller may request A, AAAA, HTTPS, SRV, MX, TXT, or other record types depending on protocol.
Modern clients often race IPv6 and IPv4 connection attempts after resolution.
why: DNS decouples service names from changing network addresses and hosting providers.
failures: Literal IPs bypass most DNS behavior; malformed names, IDNA conversion, or search-suffix rules can change the queried name.

nodes.title: Resolver API
nodes.purpose: The application delegates name lookup to the OS or language resolver.

details.summary: Most applications call a resolver API rather than constructing DNS packets themselves.
what: The API may combine DNS with local host databases and policy.
It can return multiple candidate addresses ordered by local preference.
why: Centralizing resolution lets the OS enforce local policy, enterprise configuration, VPN rules, and address-family preferences.
outputs: Canonical query name or local answer
failures: Language runtimes and containers may use different resolver stacks than the host, so observed behavior can differ from system tools.

nodes.title: Local Policy
nodes.purpose: Hosts files, search suffixes, split DNS, and caches may answer before public DNS.

details.summary: The local resolver applies host mappings, name-service order, search domains, VPN or enterprise policy, and local cache.
what: Short names may expand through search domains.
Hosts files can override DNS.
VPNs and containers can route specific zones to different resolvers.
why: Local policy supports private networks, development overrides, and operational control.
outputs: Local answer or DNS question for a recursive resolver
failures: A stale local override can make one machine disagree with everyone else.

nodes.title: Stub Query
nodes.purpose: The client resolver sends a compact DNS question to a recursive resolver.

details.summary: The stub resolver asks a configured recursive resolver to resolve the name on its behalf.
what: Queries usually use UDP first, with TCP for truncation or policy.
Encrypted transports such as DoT or DoH may be used depending on the client and network.
why: Stub resolvers keep clients simple and let recursive resolvers provide shared caching and policy.
outputs: DNS packet or encrypted DNS request
failures: Blocked UDP, captive portals, DNS interception, or misconfigured resolvers can fail before the DNS hierarchy is reached.

nodes.title: Recursive Cache
nodes.purpose: The recursive resolver answers immediately when it has a valid cached result.

details.summary: Recursive resolvers cache positive and negative answers until TTL or negative-cache policy expires.
what: A cache hit avoids root, TLD, and authoritative queries.
A cache miss starts iterative resolution through the DNS hierarchy.
why: Shared caching makes DNS fast and dramatically reduces authoritative server load.
outputs: Cached response or iterative lookup plan
failures: Stale caches, poisoned responses, or aggressive negative caching can make DNS changes appear delayed.

nodes.title: Root Referral
nodes.purpose: Root name servers point the resolver toward the relevant top-level domain.

details.summary: On a cache miss, the recursive resolver starts from known root hints and receives a referral to the TLD servers.
what: Root servers do not know every host record.
They delegate responsibility to TLD name servers such as .com, .org, or country-code TLDs.
why: Delegation lets DNS scale globally without a single database answering all names.
inputs: Question for a fully qualified domain name
Root hints or cached root NS set
outputs: NS records and glue addresses for the TLD
failures: Root reachability issues are rare, but broken local networks or blocked DNS can prevent this first referral.

nodes.title: TLD Referral
nodes.purpose: The TLD points the resolver to the domain's authoritative name servers.

details.summary: The TLD zone delegates a registered domain to its authoritative name servers.
what: The response commonly includes NS records and glue for in-bailiwick name servers.
The resolver follows the delegation to the zone authority.
why: Registries can delegate each domain while domain owners control their own zone records.
failures: Bad delegation, missing glue, or mismatched registrar and zone settings can break resolution before the authoritative zone answers.
source: external: NS and glue record behavior

nodes.title: Authoritative Answer
nodes.purpose: The zone's authoritative server returns the requested records or a negative answer.

details.summary: The authoritative server for the zone answers with records such as A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, TXT, or NXDOMAIN/NODATA.
what: CNAME responses may require additional lookups for the target name.
Responses include TTLs that guide cache lifetime.
why: The authoritative zone is the source of truth for names delegated to that domain.
outputs: Resource records, CNAME chain, delegation, or negative response
failures: Incorrect zone records, expired DNSSEC signatures, or missing CNAME targets can make authoritative data unusable.

nodes.title: Alias Chain
nodes.purpose: CNAME records may redirect the resolver to another canonical name.

details.summary: A CNAME response says the requested name is an alias, so the resolver must resolve the canonical target.
what: The final answer may include both the alias chain and address records.
Long or looping alias chains can cause failures.
why: Aliases let services move between providers or consolidate naming without changing callers.
outputs: Follow-up DNS question or completed answer chain
failures: CNAME loops, excessive chain length, and missing target records prevent usable resolution.

nodes.title: DNSSEC Validation
nodes.purpose: Validating resolvers check cryptographic proof for signed zones.

details.summary: When enabled, DNSSEC validation verifies that signed responses chain back to trusted keys.
what: The resolver checks signatures and denial-of-existence proofs.
Validation failure converts a seemingly present answer into an error for clients.
why: DNSSEC defends against forged DNS data for signed zones.
failures: Clock skew, expired signatures, bad DS records, and middleboxes can cause validation failures.

nodes.title: Answer Package
nodes.purpose: The recursive resolver assembles the response returned to the client.

details.summary: The response includes the requested records, aliases, TTLs, response code, and sometimes additional records.
what: Positive answers carry record TTLs.
Negative answers may be cached according to SOA-derived policy.
The resolver may set flags indicating recursion and validation status.
why: The client needs both the data and the metadata that controls reuse and trust.
failures: Large responses may be truncated over UDP and retried over TCP.
source: external: TTL and negative caching behavior

nodes.title: Negative Cache
nodes.purpose: NXDOMAIN and no-data results can be cached too.

details.summary: Resolvers cache some negative answers so repeated lookups for missing names do not hammer authoritative servers.
what: NXDOMAIN means the name does not exist.
NODATA means the name exists but lacks the requested record type.
why: Negative caching protects DNS infrastructure and speeds repeated failed lookups.
failures: After adding a missing record, clients may still see failure until negative cache state expires.

nodes.title: Client Cache
nodes.purpose: The OS, browser, or application may reuse the answer locally.

details.summary: After the recursive response returns, local layers may cache the answer according to TTL or their own policy.
what: Browsers and runtimes may maintain separate caches from the OS.
Some applications pin resolved addresses for connection pools.
why: Local caching reduces latency for repeated connections and smooths short network interruptions.
failures: Multiple cache layers explain why flushing one cache may not change application behavior.
source: external: browser and OS DNS cache behavior

nodes.title: Connect To Address
nodes.purpose: The application uses resolved endpoints to start the actual protocol connection.

details.summary: DNS resolution ends by handing candidate addresses back to the application, which then connects using its application protocol.
what: The client may try IPv6 and IPv4 candidates in parallel or sequence.
TLS and HTTP still validate host names even after DNS returns an address.
why: DNS only finds candidate network locations; it does not prove the application service is healthy or authorized.
failures: Successful DNS can still lead to connection refusal, TLS mismatch, routing failure, or application-level errors.

nodes.title: Transport Retry
nodes.purpose: DNS transport handles packet loss, truncation, and alternate resolver attempts.

details.summary: Resolvers retry queries, switch servers, or fall back to TCP when responses are lost or too large.
what: UDP responses can be truncated.
Clients may try multiple configured recursive resolvers.
DoH and DoT use different connection failure modes.
why: DNS must work across unreliable networks without making applications own every retry detail.
outputs: Retry, alternate resolver query, TCP fallback, or failure
failures: Firewalls and middleboxes can make one transport fail while another succeeds.

nodes.title: Debugging DNS
nodes.purpose: Separates naming failures from resolver, authority, cache, transport, and application failures.

details.summary: Good DNS debugging identifies which layer answered, whether the result was cached, and whether the failure is DNS or post-DNS connection behavior.
what: Compare local resolver results with direct authoritative or public recursive queries.
Check TTLs, CNAME chains, DNSSEC validation, split DNS, and negative cache state.
Confirm that a resolved address actually accepts the intended protocol.
why: Many outages blamed on DNS are really cache, delegation, validation, network, or application endpoint problems.
outputs: Likely failing layer and next diagnostic step
failures: Using only one lookup tool can hide differences between OS resolver behavior and raw DNS queries.

overview.title: How DNS Works
overview.purpose: A deep visual map of name resolution from application request to network connection.
overview.summary: DNS resolution starts with an application asking a local resolver for a name, passes through local policy and recursive caching, walks DNS delegation from root to TLD to authoritative servers when needed, validates and packages the answer, then returns records that the application uses to connect.
overview.why: DNS is familiar but layered; this example shows how visual architecture docs make protocol boundaries, caches, and failure modes visible.
points: Local policy and cache may answer before public DNS is involved.
Recursive resolvers hide iterative root-to-TLD-to-authority traversal from clients.
TTL, CNAMEs, DNSSEC, negative caching, and transport retries explain many surprising behaviors.

client.title: Client-Side Resolution
client.purpose: Show what happens before a recursive resolver walks the public DNS hierarchy.
client.summary: Applications usually call an OS or runtime resolver, which applies local policy, host overrides, search suffixes, cache state, and recursive resolver configuration.
client.why: Many DNS surprises are local: the public authoritative record can be correct while one client still sees a different answer.
points: Hosts files and split DNS can override public records.
Language and container resolver behavior may differ from host tools.
Local cache and connection pools can outlive record changes.

authority.title: Authority Walk
authority.purpose: Trace the recursive resolver's path to the source of truth.
authority.summary: On a cache miss, the recursive resolver follows delegation from root to TLD to authoritative zone, resolving aliases and collecting records with TTL metadata.
authority.why: The hierarchy explains both DNS scalability and where domain configuration errors enter the flow.
points: TLDs delegate registered domains to authoritative name servers.
Authoritative zones return records, aliases, or negative answers.

debugging.title: Debugging DNS
debugging.purpose: Identify whether failure belongs to local policy, cache, transport, authority, validation, or the application connection.
debugging.summary: DNS debugging works best when each lookup is tied to the resolver used, cache state, TTLs, authority data, validation status, and the post-DNS connection attempt.
debugging.why: A correct DNS answer can still lead to a failed service connection, while an incorrect client answer may come from a cache or split-DNS rule.
points: Compare OS resolver behavior with direct DNS queries.
Check CNAME chains, TTLs, negative caches, and DNSSEC validation.
Separate DNS resolution success from TCP, TLS, and application-layer success.
